prompt: Many countries spend large amounts of public money on hosting international sporting events. Some people believe that this money is wasted. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay:
Hosting a World Cup or an Olympic Games now costs the host nation billions, and the bill is paid by taxpayers most of whom will never attend an event. I agree that much of this spending is wasted, though I would argue that the waste lies in what gets built rather than in the decision to host.

The strongest case against hosting is the record of what is left behind. Stadiums designed for a fortnight of capacity crowds are handed to cities with no permanent use for them, and their upkeep falls on local budgets for decades afterwards. The promised tourism boom is harder to detect than the bid documents suggest, partly because ordinary visitors avoid a city during the event itself. Money committed to these projects is also money not committed to housing or hospitals, and that trade-off is rarely put to voters in those terms before a bid is submitted.

There are real returns, but they are narrower than supporters claim. Transport links and drainage built for an event outlast it and serve residents afterwards, and a well-run tournament can change how a country is perceived, which has value that is genuine even if it resists measurement. The difficulty is that these gains come from the infrastructure and the organisation rather than from the ceremony, and they can usually be obtained without the ceremony.

My conclusion is that the waste is avoidable rather than inherent. A country that builds only what it would have wanted anyway, and hires venues instead of erecting them, can host well. A country that treats the event as a reason to build monuments is wasting public money, and most hosts, faced with that choice, have chosen the second path.
title: Whether hosting global sporting events wastes money
